title: A Revolt Against Education
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: This article traces the history of the organized summer camp movement as a 140-year-long popular revolt against the form of schooling, arguing that the movement's persistence and scale reveal a deep public dissatisfaction with what conventional schools do to children. Beginning with Ernest Balch's Camp Chocorua in 1881 — explicitly designed to meet 'special educational needs' through participatory, physical, self-governed experience — the author shows how camp emerged as an alternative educational environment built around the original etymological meanings of learning, teaching, school, and education: motion, leisure, drawing forth, and guiding through experience. The article argues that modern cognitive science has been catching up to what camp practitioners intuited — that children learn better when they are active, embodied, and genuinely at stake in their communities. The piece closes by asking why schools, despite all evidence, continue to look nothing like the environments that 26 million Americans per year voluntarily choose for their children's summer months.
points: The organized summer camp movement — 140 years old, 26 million participants annually, and growing from 11 camps in 1895 to over 15,000 today — represents a sustained mass revolt against conventional schooling's form, not a fringe alternative.

Harvard's former president Charles Eliot declared in 1922 that 'the organized summer camp is the most important step in education that America has given the world' — a verdict that reflects how differently those outside schools evaluated the two models.

The original words for learning, teaching, school, and education all implied motion and lived experience: tracking through the world, guiding beside, leisure given back to the person, drawing forth what is already inside — all systematically reversed by institutional schooling.

Cognitive science has been catching up for decades to what camp practitioners built intuitively: physical movement, genuine stakes in a real community, self-governance, and risk-taking are not supplements to learning but its natural habitat for children.

If 26 million people a year pay to send their children somewhere that looks nothing like school, the question is not whether alternatives work but why schools persist in looking the way they do despite the evidence.
quotes: In 1881, a Dartmouth student named Ernest Balch founded Camp Chocorua on Squam Lake in New Hampshire — the first organized summer camp in America. In his own words, he deliberately planned it 'to meet special educational needs' of the students who attended. Participatory, physical, ungraded, contributory. The boys governed themselves, cooked, cleared trails, built things.

By 1895 there were 11 camps in the United States. By 1918 there were more than 1,000. By 1922, Harvard's former president Charles Eliot had seen enough of what the model produced to say plainly: 'the organized summer camp is the most important step in education that America has given the world.'

The word camp comes from the Latin campus — which means field. Open ground. Boundless space. It's the same root that gives us the word campus, which universities adopted to signal something about the relationship between learning and open space that the institution then spent centuries systematically enclosing.

Learning — to follow a track, to move through the world finding your way. Teaching — the paidagogos walking beside the child through actual experience. School — skhole, leisure, time freed from production and given back to the person to use for becoming. Education — educere, to lead out, to draw forth what is already inside. Every one of them implied motion.

What Balch built — and what 26 million people a year are still paying for — is an environment where those words still mean what they originally meant. Less a curriculum. More a set of conditions. Real participation. Practice over performance. Fun as the foundation. Bodies in motion.

That's a mass movement. That's not a fringe idea preserved by idealists on islands. That's 140 years of parents looking at what school was doing to their children and paying to send them somewhere else for the summer.
